Description: explicit — omitted glyphs field, text renders in wrong font
prompt: My MapLibre GL JS stylesheet has no `glyphs` property set at all, and my symbol layers have `text-font` set to a font name. Text labels are showing up, but in a generic font, not the one I specified. Is this a bug I need to fix, or expected behavior? What's actually happening?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Short answer **It’s not a bug – it’s the expected “local‑fonts” fallback that MapLibre GL JS has used since v5.11 when the style has no `glyphs` URL.** When the style does not point at a glyph‑PBF server, MapLibre treats every entry in `text‑font` exactly like a CSS `font‑family` list: 1. **If the named font is available on the page (via a `` to a web‑font, an `@font-face` rule, or a system font that the browser knows),** that font will be used. 2. **If the font cannot be found,** the browser falls back to its default sans‑serif (or whatever the OS supplies), which is why you see a “generic” font. So the map is working as designed; the only thing missing is the actual font you asked for. --- ## What’s really happening under the hood | Step | What MapLibre does | Why it matters for you | |------|--------------------|------------------------| | **Style parsing** | No `glyphs` field → *local‑fonts mode* is activated. | MapLibre will not try to download `.pbf` glyph ranges at all. | | **Layer rendering** | For each `text-font` entry it builds a CSS‑like font‑family list. | The order you write in `text-font` is the order of fallback, just like CSS. | | **Font resolution** | The browser’s font‑matching engine looks for a matching font family.
*If found* → the glyphs are rasterised on‑the‑fly with TinySDF (no network request).
*If not found* → the browser falls back to its default UI font. | The “generic” font you see is the browser’s default because it couldn’t locate the name you supplied. | | **CJK special case** | `localIdeographFontFamily` (default: `'sans-serif'`) is used for ideographs (Chinese/Japanese/Korean). `text-font` is ignored for those code‑points (only weight matters). | Even if you list a CJK font, it will be ignored unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily` to a specific CJK font you have loaded. | | **Error handling** | If a glyph‑PBF request ever fails (e.g. you later add a `glyphs` URL but a range 0‑255 is missing), MapLibre falls back to the same local‑font path for that range and logs a warning. | This is a *cosmetic* fallback, not a failure of the whole tile. | > **Key point:** The fallback is **client‑side only**. It works in GL JS because the browser can render any installed font with TinySDF. MapLibre **Native** does **not** have this fallback; it still requires a `glyphs` URL or a `font-faces` configuration. --- ## How to get the exact font you want ### 1. Load the font yourself (the simplest fix) ```html ``` ```js // style snippet { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"], "text-font": ["MyBrand", "Roboto Regular"], // first that exists will be used "text-size": 12 } } ``` *Make sure the string you put in `text-font` **exactly matches** the `font-family` name you defined in CSS.* If the font loads correctly, MapLibre will render the labels with that font (still using TinySDF, but the shape will be yours). ### 2. Use a glyph‑PBF server (the classic MapLibre way) If you prefer the “original” MapLibre approach—serve pre‑computed SDF glyphs—add a `glyphs` URL to the style: ```json { "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", ... } ``` *Steps:* 1. **Pick a source** – either copy the existing OpenMapTiles `fonts/` tree, use the public demo server (`https://demotiles.maplibre.org/font/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`), or generate your own PBFs with **Font Maker** or **fontnik** from a TTF/OTF. 2. **Make the folder names match** the exact strings you use in `text-font`. Example: `text-font: ["Roboto Regular"]` → you need a folder `Roboto%20Regular/` on the server. 3. **Deploy the static files** (they’re just small `.pbf` files, ~10 KB per 256‑code‑point range). 4. **Update the style** with the new `glyphs` URL. Now the map will request glyph ranges from the server, and you’ll see the exact font regardless of what the client has installed. ### 3. CJK characters (special handling) - **Default** (`localIdeographFontFamily: 'sans-serif'`): CJK glyphs are generated locally, *ignoring* `text-font`. - **If you want a specific CJK font** (e.g. Noto Sans CJK SC) you can set: ```js const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: myStyle, localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", sans-serif' // must be a web‑font you loaded }); ``` - **If you really need served CJK glyphs** (rare, slower, larger network load) set `localIdeographFontFamily: false`. Then the `glyphs` server will be used for CJK as well. ### 4. Non‑Latin scripts that need shaping (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Khmer…) - **Arabic / Hebrew** – you must also load the RTL text plugin: ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js', null, true ); ``` - **Devanagari, Khmer, etc.** – MapLibre currently **does not support complex shaping** (no HarfBuzz). Even with the correct glyph PBFs the text will look broken. The only workaround today is to avoid those scripts in map labels or pre‑render them as images/sprites. --- ## Quick checklist to diagnose the “generic font” you’re seeing | ✅ | Check | Why it matters | |----|-------|----------------| | 1 | **Is the font file actually loaded in the page?** Open DevTools → Network → filter “font”. | If the request is missing or 404, the browser can’t use it. | | 2 | **Does the `font-family` name match exactly?** (case‑sensitive, spaces, etc.) | `text-font: ["Roboto Regular"]` must match `font-family: 'Roboto Regular'`. | | 3 | **Is the style’s `glyphs` field omitted?** | If omitted, MapLibre will *always* use the local‑font fallback. | | 4 | **Are you using CJK characters?** | They ignore `text-font` unless you set `localIdeographFontFamily`. | | 5 | **Do you need RTL shaping?** | Load the RTL plugin; otherwise Arabic/Hebrew will appear left‑to‑right and may look wrong. | | 6 | **Are you on MapLibre Native?** | Native does not support the omit‑`glyphs` fallback; you must use `font-faces` or a glyph server. | If all the above are satisfied and the font still looks generic, the most common cause is **the font simply isn’t available to the browser** (e.g., you referenced a system font that the user’s OS doesn’t have). In that case you need to provide a web‑font version yourself. --- ## TL;DR - **No `glyphs` → MapLibre GL JS falls back to the browser’s font‑resolution mechanism.** - The “generic” font you see means the browser couldn’t find the font name you gave. - **Fixes:** 1. Load the desired font via `` or `@font-face` (and make the name match). 2. Or add a proper `glyphs` URL and serve the corresponding `.pbf` files. 3. For CJK, adjust `localIdeographFontFamily` if you want a specific on‑device font. 4. For Arabic/Hebrew, also load the RTL text plugin. All of this is expected behavior; it’s not a bug in MapLibre. Once you supply the font (either locally or via a glyph server) the labels will render with the exact typeface you specified.

Description: implicit — offline/local fonts on MapLibre Native, not GL JS
prompt: I'm building an offline map app with MapLibre Native on Android and want labels to render in local device fonts without running a glyphs server. What's the right way to configure this?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
## TL;DR  
**MapLibre Native (Android) → use the `font-faces` property** to point every `text‑font` name that appears in your style to a **local TTF/OTF file** (bundled with the app) together with the **Unicode ranges** that the file actually covers.  
You still have to keep a dummy `glyphs` URL in the style (it is required by the spec), but the renderer will ignore it and will read the glyphs directly from the local files you declared.

Below is a step‑by‑step guide, a minimal working example, and a checklist of common gotchas.

---

## 1. Why `font‑faces` and not the `glyphs` URL?

| SDK | How it gets glyphs when you **don’t** run a glyph server |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|
| **MapLibre GL JS (≥ 5.11)** | Falls back automatically to the browser’s local fonts (TinySDF) when `glyphs` is omitted **or** when a PBF fails to load. |
| **MapLibre Native (Android / iOS)** | **Never** falls back to system fonts. The style *must* contain a `glyphs` URL (any reachable URL) **and** a `font-faces` block that maps each `text‑font` name to one or more local font files. The `font-faces` block is the only way to render offline without a glyph server. |

> **Bottom line:** on Android you *must* use `font-faces`. The `glyphs` field can point at a placeholder (e.g. `https://example.com/placeholder/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`) – it will never be consulted as long as the `font-faces` mapping is present and correct.

---

## 2. High‑level workflow

1. **Pick the fonts you want to use** (e.g. Noto Sans, Noto Sans Arabic, Noto Sans CJK SC).  
2. **Copy the TTF/OTF files into your app** (`app/src/main/assets/fonts/…` or `res/raw`).  
3. **Determine the Unicode ranges each font covers** (see § 3).  
4. **Add a `font-faces` block to your style JSON** that maps the `text-font` name(s) to the local file(s) and the ranges.  
5. **Reference the same `text-font` names in your layer definitions** (`text-font: ["Noto Sans Regular", "Noto Sans Arabic Regular"]`).  
6. **Load the style** (local or remote) as usual – the renderer will read the glyphs from the bundled files.  

---

## 3. Figuring out Unicode ranges

`font-faces` needs an explicit list of *code‑point ranges* that each file supplies. A range is a string `"start-end"` where `start` and `end` are **hexadecimal** Unicode code points (inclusive).  

### 3.1 Quick‑and‑dirty approach (good enough for most Noto families)

Noto fonts are already split by script, so you can use the script’s official Unicode block(s). Example:

| Font file | Script | Typical range(s) (hex) |
|-----------|--------|------------------------|
| `NotoSans-Regular.ttf` | Latin, Greek, Cyrillic | `0000-00FF,0100-024F,0370-03FF,0400-04FF` |
| `NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf` | Arabic | `0600-06FF,0750-077F,08A0-08FF,FB50-FDFF,FE70-FEFF` |
| `NotoSansDevanagari-Regular.ttf` | Devanagari | `0900-097F` |
| `NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf` | CJK Simplified | `4E00-9FFF,3400-4DBF,F900-FAFF` (plus extensions if you need them) |

If you want to be precise, you can generate the list automatically:

```bash
# Install fonttools (pip install fonttools)
python - <<'PY'
import sys, json, pathlib
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont

def ranges_from_font(path):
    font = TTFont(path)
    cmap = font.getBestCmap()
    codepoints = sorted(cmap.keys())
    # Collapse consecutive codepoints into ranges
    ranges = []
    start = prev = codepoints[0]
    for cp in codepoints[1:]:
        if cp == prev + 1:
            prev = cp
            continue
        ranges.append((start, prev))
        start = prev = cp
    ranges.append((start, prev))
    # Convert to "xxxx-yyyy" strings
    return [f"{s:04X}-{e:04X}" for s, e in ranges]

font_path = pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
print(json.dumps(ranges_from_font(font_path), indent=2))
PY
  fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf
```

Copy the resulting array into the style (see § 4).

---

## 4. Minimal style JSON with `font-faces`

Below is a **complete, self‑contained** style snippet that you can drop into `assets/style.json` (or serve from a local web server). It demonstrates:

* a dummy `glyphs` URL (required but never used)
* a `font-faces` block that points at three local fonts
* a `text` layer that falls back from Latin → Arabic → CJK

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "glyphs": "https://example.com/placeholder/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf",
  "sources": {
    "osm": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "https://example.com/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    },
    {
      "id": "place-labels",
      "type": "symbol",
      "source": "osm",
      "source-layer": "place",
      "layout": {
        "text-field": ["get", "name"],
        "text-font": [
          "Noto Sans Regular",
          "Noto Sans Arabic Regular",
          "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular"
        ],
        "text-size": 14,
        "text-anchor": "center"
      },
      "paint": {
        "text-color": "#222"
      }
    }
  ],

  /* -------------------------------------------------
   *  FONT‑FACES – map each logical font name to a local file
   * ------------------------------------------------- */
  "font-faces": [
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Regular",
      "src": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSans-Regular.ttf",
      "unicode-range": [
        "0000-00FF", "0100-024F", "0370-03FF", "0400-04FF"
      ]
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans Arabic Regular",
      "src": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf",
      "unicode-range": [
        "0600-06FF", "0750-077F", "08A0-08FF",
        "FB50-FDFF", "FE70-FEFF"
      ]
    },
    {
      "font-family": "Noto Sans CJK SC Regular",
      "src": "file:///android_asset/fonts/NotoSansCJKsc-Regular.otf",
      "unicode-range": [
        "4E00-9FFF", "3400-4DBF", "F900-FAFF"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

### How the `src` works

* `file:///android_asset/...` points at the **`assets/`** folder of the APK.  
* If you prefer `res/raw`, use `android.resource://your.package.name/raw/font_name` (e.g. `android.resource://com.example.myapp/raw/noto_sans`).

> **Important:** The path must be a *URI* that the native renderer can open with `std::ifstream`. `file:///android_asset/…` is the most straightforward.

---

## 5. Android‑side code (Kotlin)

```kotlin
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapLibreMap
import org.maplibre.android.maps.Style
import org.maplibre.android.maps.MapView

class OfflineMapActivity : AppCompatActivity() {

    private lateinit var mapView: MapView

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        MapLibre.getInstance(this)   // initialise the SDK once
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_offline_map)

        mapView = findViewById(R.id.mapView)
        mapView.onCreate(savedInstanceState)

        // Load the style that lives in assets/style.json
        mapView.getMapAsync { mapboxMap: MapLibreMap ->
            mapboxMap.setStyle(
                Style.Builder()
                    .fromUri("asset://style.json")   // <-- our JSON above
            ) { style ->
                // map is ready – you can add sources, layers, etc.
            }
        }
    }

    // … forward lifecycle callbacks to mapView (onStart, onResume, …)
}
```

*No extra SDK calls are needed* – once the style is parsed, the native renderer will automatically read the `font-faces` block and use the bundled fonts.

---

## 6. What about CJK ideographs?

* **Native does not have the `localIdeographFontFamily` shortcut** that GL JS uses.  
* If you want CJK characters to render **offline**, you **must** list a CJK font in `font-faces` (as shown above).  
* The CJK font you bundle should be a **system‑installed font** (e.g. Noto Sans CJK SC) or any other OTF/TTF that contains the needed glyphs.  
* Because CJK ranges are huge, the file can be large (≈ 10 MB). If you are okay with the on‑device TinySDF fallback (which is *fast* but uses the generic system sans‑serif), you can **omit the CJK entry** from `font-faces`. The renderer will then fall back to the device’s default CJK font automatically (this is the same behaviour GL JS uses when `localIdeographFontFamily` is left at its default).  

> **Decision point:**  
> *If you need *exact* visual parity with a specific CJK font (e.g. brand‑specific glyph shapes), add it to `font-faces`.  
> *If you just need readable CJK and want to keep the APK size small, **don’t** add a CJK entry – the native engine will use the device’s built‑in CJK font.*

---

## 7. Scripts that need shaping (Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Khmer …)

* MapLibre Native **does not perform complex text shaping** (no HarfBuzz).  
* For **Arabic & Hebrew** you must also load the **RTL text plugin** – the same plugin used by GL JS – otherwise characters will appear in logical order (right‑to‑left but not mirrored).

  ```kotlin
  MapLibre.getInstance(this, "file:///android_asset/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js")
  ```

Description: anti-pattern — porting font-faces config from Native to GL JS
prompt: I have a working `font-faces` config in my MapLibre Native app's stylesheet that renders local fonts offline with explicit Unicode ranges per file. I'm now building a MapLibre GL JS web app and want the same offline-font behavior — can I copy the same `font-faces` config into my GL JS stylesheet?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** **No.** The `font‑faces` property is a **MapLibre Native‑only** feature. GL JS does not understand it, and copying the block into a GL JS style will be ignored (or will cause a validation error). Below you’ll find a concise explanation of why it doesn’t work, what the two GL JS alternatives are, and a step‑by‑step recipe for reproducing the same “offline‑font” experience you have in Native. --- ## 1️⃣ Why `font‑faces` can’t be used in GL JS | Feature | MapLibre Native | MapLibre GL JS | |---------|----------------|----------------| | **Property name** | `font-faces` (top‑level style property) | *No such property* | | **Purpose** | Map a `text-font` name → one or more local font files **with explicit Unicode ranges** (you tell the engine which file covers which code‑points). | GL JS either **(a)** fetches pre‑computed SDF glyph PBFs from a `glyphs` URL **or** **(b)** falls back to the browser’s normal font‑fallback mechanism when `glyphs` is omitted or a glyph range fails to load. | | **Offline support** | Works out‑of‑the‑box because the files are on the device and the engine knows exactly which range to use. | No built‑in range‑mapping; you must either (i) host the glyph PBFs yourself (still a network request, but you can serve them from a local server) **or** (ii) rely on the browser’s local‑font fallback (no network at all). | | **Current status** | Implemented in Android ≥ 11.13.0, iOS ≥ 6.18.0. | **Not implemented** – see issue [#165](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-native/issues/165) (Native) and issue [#6637](https://github.com/maplibre/maplibre-gl-js/issues/6637) (GL JS). | Because GL JS and Native use **different mechanisms**, you cannot simply copy the `font-faces` block from a Native style into a GL JS style and expect it to work. --- ## 2️⃣ How to get the same “offline‑font” behaviour in GL JS There are **two supported paths**: | Path | What you get | When to use it | |------|--------------|----------------| | **A. Omit `glyphs` and load fonts locally (browser fallback)** | No network request for glyphs. Text is rendered with whatever fonts the browser can find (system fonts, or web‑fonts you load with `@font-face`). | • You control the font files (e.g. custom brand font).
• You are OK with the fact that the exact rasterisation may differ slightly between browsers/OSes (the same as any normal web page). | | **B. Self‑host the glyph‑PBF tree** | Same SDF‑glyph rendering model as Native, but you serve the `.pbf` files from a local origin (or a CDN you control). | • You need **pixel‑perfect** parity with a Native style that already uses glyph PBFs.
• You are fine with a tiny HTTP request per Unicode range (≈ 256 code‑points per request). | Below each path is a practical checklist. --- ### 📦 Path A – “Local‑fonts mode” (no `glyphs`) 1. **Remove the `glyphs` field** from your style JSON (or set it to `null`). ```json { "version": 8, "glyphs": null, // <-- important "layers": [ … ] } ``` 2. **Add the fonts you need to the page** – either as system fonts (already installed on the user’s OS) or as **web‑fonts** you ship with the app. *Web‑font example (CSS):* ```css @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand Sans"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrandSans-Regular.woff2") format("woff2"); font-weight: 400; font-style: normal; } @font-face { font-family: "MyBrand Sans"; src: url("/fonts/MyBrandSans-Bold.woff2") format("woff2"); font-weight: 700; font-style: normal; } ``` *If you need to guarantee the font is loaded before the map draws, you can use the Font Loading API:* ```js document.fonts.load('1rem "MyBrand Sans"').then(() => { // now safe to create the map initMap(); }); ``` 3. **Reference those fonts in `text-font`** exactly as you declared them in `@font-face` (or as the system‑font name). ```json { "type": "symbol", "layout": { "text-field": "{name}", "text-font": ["MyBrand Sans Regular", "MyBrand Sans Bold", "Noto Sans Regular"] } } ``` *Note:* GL JS treats the `text-font` array as a **CSS‑style fallback list**. The first name that resolves to a loaded font wins. If none resolve, the browser falls back to its generic `sans-serif` family. 4. **CJK handling (optional)** - By default GL JS generates CJK glyphs on‑device via TinySDF (`localIdeographFontFamily: 'sans-serif'`). - If you want a nicer on‑device CJK font, set the map option: ```js const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: styleUrl, localIdeographFontFamily: '"Noto Sans CJK SC", "Noto Sans CJK JP", sans-serif' }); ``` - **Do not** try to serve CJK glyph PBFs unless you explicitly set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` (which forces network requests and is usually slower). 5. **RTL scripts** – If you need Arabic, Hebrew, etc., load the RTL text plugin (still required even in local‑fonts mode): ```js import { setRTLTextPlugin } from 'maplibre-gl'; setRTLTextPlugin( 'https://unpkg.com/maplibre-gl/dist/maplibre-gl-rtl-text.js', null, true ); ``` 6. **Result** – All text is rendered locally, offline, without any glyph‑PBF server. The only “range” control you have is the **font file itself** (you can ship a subset of a font if you want to keep the download size tiny). --- ### 📦 Path B – “Self‑hosted glyph PBFs” If you need **exactly the same SDF glyphs** that Native uses (e.g. you have a strict visual spec or you want the same rasterisation on every platform), follow these steps: 1. **Obtain the glyph PBF tree** for every font you use. - For common fonts (Noto, Open Sans, Roboto, etc.) you can copy the pre‑built tree from the **OpenMapTiles fonts repo** or **UNDP‑Data/fonts**. - For a custom TTF/OTF, generate the PBFs with **Font Maker** or **fontnik**: ```bash # Example with Font Maker (Node) npx @maplibre/font-maker \ --font-path ./MyBrandSans-Regular.ttf \ --output ./fonts/MyBrandSans-Regular ``` This creates the folder structure `MyBrandSans-Regular/{range}.pbf`. 2. **Serve the files** from a URL that matches the style’s `glyphs` template. Example folder layout on your server (`https://my.cdn.com/fonts/`): ``` /fonts/ MyBrand Sans Regular/ 0-255.pbf 256-511.pbf … Noto Sans Regular/ 0-255.pbf … ``` 3. **Set the `glyphs` field** in the GL JS style to point at that base URL: ```json { "glyphs": "https://my.cdn.com/fonts/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf", "layers": [ … ] } ``` 4. **Make sure the `text-font` names match the folder names exactly** (including spaces, case, and weight suffixes). ```json "text-font": ["MyBrand Sans Regular", "Noto Sans Regular"] ``` 5. **CJK** – As with Path A, GL JS will still use the local‑ideograph fallback unless you disable it: ```js const map = new maplibregl.Map({ container: 'map', style: styleUrl, localIdeographFontFamily: false // forces served glyphs for CJK }); ``` *Only enable this if you have deliberately generated CJK glyph PBFs and you really need those exact shapes.* 6. **RTL** – Same as Path A, load the RTL plugin if you need Arabic/Hebrew. 7. **Result** – The map behaves exactly like Native: it requests glyph PBFs from your own origin, works offline **as long as the origin is reachable** (e.g. bundled with the app via a local HTTP server or a Service Worker cache). No `font-faces` needed. --- ## 3️⃣ Quick “cheat‑sheet” comparison | Feature | Native (`font-faces`) | GL JS – Path A (local fonts) | GL JS – Path B (self‑hosted glyphs) | |---------|----------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------------| | **Configuration key** | `font-faces` (top‑level) | *none* (`glyphs` omitted) | `glyphs` URL template | | **Unicode‑range control** | Explicit per‑file ranges | Implicit – whole font file | Implicit – whole font file (range split by server) | | **Network traffic** | None (fonts are on‑device) | None (fonts are bundled with the page) | One request per 256‑code‑point range that appears in the viewport | | **Cross‑platform parity** | Exact (same SDF) | May differ slightly (browser rendering) | Exact (same SDF) | | **CJK handling** | Same as other scripts (glyphs) | Generated locally by default (`localIdeographFontFamily`) | Served glyphs only if you set `localIdeographFontFamily: false` | | **RTL shaping** | Needs `setRTLTextPlugin` in GL JS, not needed in Native | Same plugin required | Same plugin required | | **Supported GL JS version** | N/A | ≥ 5.11.0 (fallback works) | Any version that supports `glyphs` (all) | --- ## 4️⃣ TL;DR – What you should do 1. **Do not copy `font-faces` into a GL JS style.** It will be ignored. 2. Choose one of the two GL JS approaches: - **If you just need offline rendering and can accept normal web‑font fallback**, drop the `glyphs` field, load your fonts with `@font-face`, and let GL JS use its built‑in local‑font fallback (plus `localIdeographFontFamily` for CJK if you want a nicer on‑device font). - **If you need pixel‑perfect parity with the Native app**, self‑host the glyph‑PBF tree for every font you use, point `glyphs` at that URL, and keep `localIdeographFontFamily` at its default (or disable it only if you have CJK PBFs). Both approaches work completely offline once the font files (either `.woff2`/`.ttf` or `.pbf`) are cached or bundled with the web app (e.g., via a Service Worker).
